chapters.name: Chapter 1: Planning and writing your site

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Why an athlete needs a simple website
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Decide who your site is for and what it must show.
This lesson builds toward: Before building your site, you will choose your main audience and list what they need in four sections, with About, Stats or Services, Highlights and Contact matched to that audience.
A website is a page you control. Social apps can change rules or lose your account; your site stays the same. It is also easier for a coach or brand to read than scrolling a feed.
Decide who it is for. A recruiting site needs stats, academics, highlights and coach references. A brand-focused site needs your audience, past partnerships and media kit. A coaching or camp site needs your services, schedule and sign-up.
Keep it to one page at first, with sections: About, Stats or Services, Highlights, and Contact.
Step by step:
- Pick your main audience: coaches, brands or clients.
- List what they need to see.
- Group it into four sections: About, Stats or Services, Highlights, Contact.
Words to know:
- Website: pages on the internet at an address you share, like a link.
- Section: one part of a page, with its own heading.
Try it now: Write your site's main audience and list what they need to see under the four section headings.
You can now plan a one-page athlete site for a clear audience.

check.q: What should a brand-focused athlete site show?
options: Your audience, past partnerships and media kit
check.why: Brands want to see your audience, partnerships and media kit.

check.q: You coach a youth skills camp and want a site for it. Which sections fit?
options: About, Services, Highlights and Contact with sign-up
check.why: A coaching or camp site needs services, schedule and sign-up.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing your page with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to draft your About section and section text, then edit it.
This lesson builds toward: Using your true facts and an AI assistant, you will write an About section and choose a safe contact method, with every fact checked, nothing untrue, your own voice, and no home address, phone number, full birth date or schedule.
Give an AI assistant your facts and ask for a draft: "I'm a 2027 graduate, 6'1" outside hitter, 3.6 GPA, team captain, want to study engineering. Write a 100-word About section for my recruiting website in first person, friendly and confident."
Check every fact. AI can add things that are not true, like awards you did not win. Remove anything you cannot prove and put it in your own words.
Keep private details off the page: no home address, phone number, full date of birth or school schedule. For contact, use a separate email you made for sports, or a contact form, and if you are a minor, list a parent or coach as a contact too.
Step by step:
- List your true facts.
- Ask AI for a short About section draft.
- Check every fact and remove anything untrue.
- Rewrite in your own voice.
- Decide on a safe contact method.
Words to know:
- First person: writing with "I" and "my".
- Contact form: a box on a site where visitors send you a message without seeing your email.
Try it now: Use an AI assistant to draft your About section. Check every fact, edit it into your voice, and set up a separate sports email if you do not have one.
You can now write accurate website text with AI help and choose a safe contact method.

check.q: Which detail should stay off your site?
check.why: Keep home address, phone number, full birth date and schedule off the page.

check.q: AI's draft says you were "all-state", but you were not. What do you do?
options: Ask AI to add more awards
Remove it and write only true facts
check.why: Check every fact and remove anything you cannot prove.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: SEO basics: helping Google understand your page
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a page title, headings, a short description and image alt text that help search.
This lesson builds toward: For your one-page site, you will write a page title, section headings, a short description and image alt text that help search, with your name and sport in the title, alt text on every image and no keyword stuffing.
SEO, or search engine optimization, means making your page easy for search engines like Google to understand, so the right people find it.
Google's own SEO Starter Guide recommends a few basics: a clear, unique page title (for example "Jordan Lee | Volleyball Outside Hitter, Class of 2027"), headings that organize the page, helpful, up-to-date text written for people, a short page description, and short descriptive alt text on images.
Write for people first. Do not stuff keywords; just use the words a coach or brand would type, like your name, sport, position, grad year and city or region.
Step by step:
- Write a page title with your name, sport and position or service.
- Use headings for each section.
- Write a one- to two-sentence description of the page.
- Add short alt text to every image.
- Use words your audience would search for.
Words to know:
- SEO: search engine optimization: helping search engines understand your page so people find it.
- Alt text: a short written description of an image, used by search engines and screen readers.
- Keyword: a word or phrase people type into a search engine.
Official sources:
- Google Search Central: SEO Starter Guide
Try it now: Write your page title, the four section headings, a one-sentence page description, and alt text for two photos you plan to use.
You can now write a page title, headings, description and alt text that help people find your page.

options: Helping search engines understand your page so the right people find it
Making your page load photos faster
check.why: SEO means making your page easy for search engines to understand.

check.q: You are adding a photo of yourself running a hurdle race. What alt text do you write?
options: "Sam Ortiz clearing a hurdle at the county meet"
check.why: Alt text is a short, descriptive line about the image, without stuffing keywords.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building your page in Google Sites
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build your one-page site in Google Sites.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sites, you will build a one-page site with four sections, photos, an embedded highlight video and a contact button, using only photos you have permission to use and following your school's logo rules.
Google Sites is a free website builder from Google. You need a Google account. Open sites.google.com, start a new blank site or a template, and add your sections.
Use the builder to add text boxes, images, headings and buttons, and to embed a YouTube highlight video. Pick a simple theme with your team colors and readable text. Use only photos you took or have permission to use, and follow your school's rules on logos.
Keep it clean: one page, four sections, big readable text, and one clear button to contact you or watch highlights.
Step by step:
- Go to sites.google.com and sign in.
- Start a blank site or template.
- Add your page title and four sections with headings.
- Paste your edited text.
- Add photos with alt text and embed your highlight video.
- Add one contact button or form link.
Words to know:
- Template: a ready-made layout you fill in.
- Embed: show a video or item from another site inside your page.
Try it now: Build your page in Google Sites with your title, four sections, at least one photo with alt text, and your highlight video or a placeholder.
You can now build a clean one-page athlete website in Google Sites.

check.q: Where do you go to start a Google Sites page?
check.why: Open sites.google.com and sign in with a Google account.

check.q: You want your highlight video on your site. What do you do?
options: Embed your YouTube video in the page
check.why: Google Sites can embed a YouTube highlight video.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Publishing and checking your site
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Publish your site, test it on a phone and share the link.
This lesson builds toward: When your site is ready, you will publish it, test it on a phone and share the link in your bios, with every link, button and video working and the site reviewed by a coach or parent.
When your page is ready, use the publish button and choose your site's web address. Pick a short address with your name and sport.
Test it on a phone, since most coaches and fans will open it there. Check that every link and button works, the video plays, and the text is easy to read. Ask a coach or parent to look at it too.
Share the link in your social media bios, your email signature and your recruiting profiles. If you change your contact details, update the site right away.
Step by step:
- Click publish and choose a short web address.
- Open it on a phone.
- Test every link, button and video.
- Ask a coach or parent to review it.
- Add the link to your bios and email signature.
Words to know:
- Publish: make your site live on the internet.
- URL: a web address, like the link you share.
Try it now: Publish your site, test it on a phone, ask one adult to review it, and add the link to one social profile.
You can now publish, test and share your athlete website.

check.q: What makes a good site web address?
options: Short, with your name and sport
check.why: Pick a short address with your name and sport.

check.q: You changed your sports email. What do you do with your site?
options: Update the contact details right away
check.why: If your contact details change, update the site right away.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping it fresh and checking search
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set an update routine and see how your site shows up in search.
This lesson builds toward: After publishing, you will plan an update routine and check how your site appears in search, with an update reminder after each season and a note of what appears when you search your name and sport.
Search engines and visitors both like pages that are up to date. Update your stats, highlights and schedule after each season or big event, and change the date in your About section.
New sites can take time to appear in search results. Search Google for your name plus sport and see what shows up. Google offers a free tool called Search Console that site owners can use to see how their site performs in search; the SEO Starter Guide explains it.
Every few months, ask an AI assistant: "Here is my website text. Suggest three ways to make it clearer for college coaches." Then decide what to change.
Step by step:
- Set a reminder to update after each season.
- Search your name plus sport and note what appears.
- Read about Search Console in Google's guide.
- Ask AI for three clarity suggestions and pick what to use.
Words to know:
- Search Console: Google's free tool that shows site owners how their site appears in Google Search.
- Search results: the list of pages a search engine shows for a search.
Official sources:
- Google Search Central: SEO Starter Guide
Try it now: Final task: make sure your published site has a clear title, AI-assisted and edited About text, stats and highlights, a safe contact method, image alt text and a social link to it. Search Google for your name and sport and note what shows up.
You can now keep your site fresh and check how it shows up in search.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Page title and SEO basics The title lacks your name or sport, or images have no alt text. A title with name and sport, headings for each section, a short description and alt text on every image. Uses the words the audience would search, such as position, grad year and region, without stuffing. About section Contains untrue facts or reads as copied AI text. Every fact true and checked, written in the athlete's own voice. Tailored to the main audience, such as academics and character for college coaches. Stats and highlights Missing, out of date, or uses photos without permission. Current stats and an embedded highlight video, with permitted photos only and school logo rules followed. Includes the date stats were last updated and a short caption for each highlight. Safe contact Shows a home address, personal phone number or full birth date. A sports email or contact form, plus a parent or coach contact for minors. The contact button is tested and replies go to an account checked regularly. Published, linked and checked Not published, broken links, or not linked from a profile. Published at a short address, tested on a phone, reviewed by a coach or parent and linked from one social profile. Search results for name and sport are noted and an update reminder is set. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: A free Google tool that shows how your site performs in search
check.why: Search Console lets site owners see how their site performs in search.

check.q: Your season just ended. What does your update routine say to do?
options: Update your stats, highlights and the date in your About section
check.why: Update after each season or big event so the page stays current.
